newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean union workers vow partial strike.
newsitem.headline: South Korean union workers vow partial strike.

text.p: The head of South Korea's outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions said on Thursday union workers would go on partial strike on Friday.
Kwon Young-kil, president of the confederation, said in a news conference the confederation would delay an all-out strike to see how parliament handled the revision of a new labour law.

"We hope parliament will come up with a correct labour law this time. We will wait until midnight of February 28," Kwon told reporters. A controversial new labour law rammed through parliament in late December is due to take effect on March 1.

He said member unions in the Seoul area would walk out from 1:00 p.m. (0400 GMT) to 5:00 p.m. (0800 GMT). Workers at public services, including hospitals and the Seoul subway, would not participate in the work stoppage, he said.
"Our aim is to give warnings and not trouble," said Kwon.
Striking workers would rally in central Seoul to demand that the labour law be repealed, he said.

The confederation, which claims 500,000 member workers, has said it would launch an all-out strike on Friday if their demands went ignored. They have vowed to deter the new law from taking effect from March 1.

Union leaders said they were looking for positive results from parliamentary debates in the National Assembly which reopened last week for a 30-day session. Ruling and opposition parties are discussing a possible revision of the legislation.
The confederation postponed an earlier plan to strike on February 18 to between February 24 and 28.

In a televised address on Tuesday, President Kim Young-sam apologised over the labour law but fell short of satisfying the union which wanted the law revoked. The legislation would make it easier for employers to lay off workers and replace strikers.
Kim Young-sam's New Korea party passed the law in parliament in late December, triggering nearly a month of strikes.
In a jab at the confederation's hardline stance, the nation's 30 leading business conglomerates on Wednesday agreed to freeze wage payments for 1997 at last year's level.
The Federation of Korean Industries, the lobbying body for the nation's major companies, said the wage freeze was necessary to strengthen international competitiveness.

Senior officials of the nation's 30 largest business groups, called chaebol, also said they opposed the legalisation of the confederation. They demanded that employers be allowed to lay off workers and manage working hours flexibly.
